terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent; with an accusative, dē + ablative, an accusative and infinitive, or quod; to someone, cum aliquō or apud aliquem
evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.10.7: quererer tēcum atque expostulārem
Sen. Ep. 56.7: quae nōn audit audīsse sē queritur
terms.comment: What one complains of in the accusative (injūriam querī) or with dē; the person complained to with cum or apud. It is also to lament one’s lot, and in poetry of birds’ song (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: complain at length, pour out one’s complaints
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 125: conqueritur mēcum mulier fortūnās suās
terms.comment: A fuller, louder complaining than queror.

evidence: Cic. Q. Fr. 3.8.1 (Lewis & Short): epistula plēna querēlārum
terms.comment: The usual noun; with a genitive of what it is about, querēla temporum, a complaint against the times (Cic. Fam. 2.16.1). After Augustus also a formal accusation (Petronius, the Digest).

evidence: Plaut. Men. 785: neuter ad mē īrētis cum querimōniā

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; cum aliquō (dē aliquā rē)
terms.comment: Classically to have it out with someone, cum aliquō expostulāre; later chiefly to demand urgently (Lewis & Short).
Graviter, “heavily”, with verbs of feeling: graviter ferre, take hard.

phrases.latin: quotiēns tandem ēdīxī tibi, ut cavērēs, neuter ad mē īrētis cum querimōniā?
phrases.english: How many times have I told you to make sure that neither of you came to me with a complaint?
I would complain to you and have it out with you

phrases.latin: hūc nempe versātur atque illūc, somnum inter aegritūdinēs levem captāns; quae nōn audit audīsse sē queritur
phrases.english: he tosses this way and that, trying to catch a light sleep between his worries, and complains that he has heard what he doesn’t hear
